Solar basics

Solar myths versus facts

Ten claims that circulate at barbecues and in sales pitches — sorted into what is true, what is half-true, and what is nonsense.

Published 8 October 2026Updated 15 October 20267 min readSolvanta Energy editorial

Word travels fast about solar — usually via a neighbour explaining their bill, a salesperson explaining a rebate, or a social post explaining neither. Here are the claims that recur most, with the honest version of each.

1. "Solar only works in hot, sunny places"

Panels run on light, not heat — they generate on cloudy days and in cool climates. In fact, they are slightly more efficient in the cool, clear conditions of a southern winter than in a heatwave, because high cell temperatures sap a little efficiency. Australia's solar map is generous almost everywhere the sun rises.

2. "Panels need constant cleaning to keep working"

For most Australian homes, rain keeps output close to clean-panel levels. Cleaning earns its keep mainly in dusty inland areas, coastal salt environments and under shedding trees. Monitoring tells you when soiling is actually costing you — see the maintenance article for how to judge.

3. "Solar means no more power bills"

Solar reduces the usage half of a bill dramatically in most cases, but the daily supply charge remains, night-time usage still draws on the grid (or a battery), and winter generates less while households consume more. The realistic claim is a much smaller bill, shaped by tariff and behaviour — not a zero one.

4. "A bigger system is always better"

Generation beyond what the household can use or store is exported at the feed-in rate, which is well below the retail price displaced by self-consumption. Size to consumption first; grow the system for a battery, a vehicle or an electrification plan, not for its own sake.

5. "Batteries are set-and-forget forever"

Batteries need sensible placement (heat is the enemy), have a warranted throughput limit that heavy cycling can approach, and a realistic service life defined in their warranty terms. They are low-maintenance, not maintenance-free or eternal.

6. "Solar keeps the house running during a blackout"

Standard grid-connected systems must shut down within seconds of an outage — anti-islanding protection that keeps linesworkers safe. Keeping power on requires a battery with backup wiring, planned at design time. This surprise is common enough to have its own article.

7. "All quotes are basically the same — just compare the price"

Quotes differ most where the eye cannot see: inverter type, panel performance curves, protection components, monitoring, labour scope and warranty labour coverage. Two similar prices can buy quite different twenty-year outcomes; the comparison table in our buying guide shows what to line up.

8. "The rebate is a cheque from the government"

Federal support works through small-scale technology certificates: the certificates are created at installation and their value is discounted from your invoice by the installer, who handles the paperwork. From 1 May 2026, battery support also tapers by installed capacity. The rebates guide links to the official sources for the current rules.

9. "Solar will damage my roof"

Properly installed mounting is engineered for the roof type, with sealed penetrations and load paths, and panels actually shield the roofing beneath them from direct sun and hail. What causes roof trouble is poor workmanship, aged roof coverings that should have been renewed first, and installation onto a roof that was already failing. Roof condition is a design conversation for exactly this reason.

10. "You have to be home to get the benefit of solar"

Generation is automatic; presence only changes how much of it is self-consumed. Households that are out during the day export more and save less per kilowatt hour — which is precisely what timers, delayed starts, daytime charging and batteries are for. Behaviour shifts the split between cheap exports and full-price avoided imports.

How to check the next bold claim you hear

  • Ask what assumptions sit under the number — rates, usage, self-consumption, generation per kilowatt.
  • Ask whether the claim is general or specific to your property. Generic promises about specific houses are a contradiction.
  • Check the official sources: the Clean Energy Regulator for federal schemes, your state's energy department for state programs, the AER's Energy Made Easy for tariffs.
  • Treat urgency as a warning sign. Real programs have official deadlines you can verify; invented ones expire when you leave the room.

Key takeaways

  • Panels run on light, prefer cool clear days, and keep working through cloud at reduced output.
  • Cleaning is situational; big bills are dominated by usage rates, not dust.
  • Bills get smaller, not zero — supply charges and night usage remain.
  • Outage power needs a battery and backup wiring; standard solar legally shuts down.
  • Where a claim meets a price, demand the assumptions — and check official sources.
